unresolved_must_fix.claim: The revision cut the sentence about the people met at Cambridge House. As a result, 'They were largely diplomatic' now follows a sentence about Lady Palmerston and has no antecedent.
unresolved_must_fix.counterevidence: Context implies guests at her evenings, but no plural noun is available.

evidence.quote: The people one met there were never smart and seldom young; they were largely diplomatic, and diplomats are commonly dull
The people one met there were never smart and seldom young. They were largely diplomatic, and diplomats are commonly dull.
Lady Palmerston was no longer young or handsome. They were largely diplomatic, and diplomats are commonly dull.

unresolved_must_fix.minimal_repair: Restore 'The people one met there were never smart and seldom young.' before 'They were largely diplomatic'.
unresolved_must_fix.reader_effect: The pronoun reads as referring to Lady Palmerston or her evenings. This muddles the catalogue of dull guests that makes her success a riddle.
unresolved_must_fix.title: Orphan 'They' in Cambridge House description

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The revision cut 'No professional diplomatists worried about falsehoods.' This leaves the paradox directly after 'Yet the diplomatic standard of trust…' with no bridge.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: P8's 'Diplomatists have no right to complain of mere lies' partly restores the logic afterward.

evidence.quote: No professional diplomatists worried about falsehoods. Words were with them forms of expression which varied with individuals
No professional diplomatists worried about falsehoods. The worst liars were the candid.
Yet the diplomatic standard of trust seemed to be other than the parliamentarian. The worst liars were the candid.

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Reinsert 'No professional diplomatists worried about falsehoods.' before the paradox.
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: The aphorism becomes a non sequitur. Its point, that diplomats discount words and fear motives, now arrives only later with the traps line.
unresolved_should_improve.title: 'The worst liars were the candid' loses its premise

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The first draft kept the condition that French verse demands knowledge and a fine ear, and that 'Adams had neither'. The revision cuts this, so the de Musset evasion has no motive and the failure rests only on 'bored him'.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: 'He knew he was no companion for Swinburne' still conveys inferiority.

evidence.quote: it requires extraordinary knowledge of the language and rare refinement of ear to appreciate even the recitation of French verse
Appreciating French verse requires extraordinary knowledge of the language and rare refinement of ear, and Adams had neither.
Swinburne tested him then and there by one of his favorite tests--Victor Hugo. Adams tried to evade Swinburne's vehement insistence by parading an affection for Alfred de Musset.

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's one-sentence 'Appreciating French verse… Adams had neither.'
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: Adams's self-condemnation reads as mere taste. The source grounds it in a sensory and educational incapacity, which feeds 'One who could feel neither Hugo nor Landor was lost'.
unresolved_should_improve.title: Hugo test loses the reason for Adams's failure
